authored_explainer.title: Cereal Production Rose 1.5x; Farmland Rankings Explain Less
authored_explainer.hook: Cereal production climbed 1.5 times while land area told a different story.
says: Progression to secondary school rose from 77.8% in 1985 to 91.3% in 2017. More students reached the next level.
Cereal production rose from 1083.7 million metric tons in 1972 to 1644.1 in 2024. The world harvested far more grain.
China has 5.2 million square kilometers of farmland; the United States 4.2, Australia 3.6, Brazil 2.4, Russia 2.2. Land alone does not determine harvests.
authored_explainer.closing: Food supply depends on what farmland produces, not simply how much land a country has.
authored_explainer.question: What drove the bigger harvest?

authored_explainer.title: Waste Energy Reached 30.1% While Methane Kept Rising
authored_explainer.hook: Waste energy reached 30.1%, but its methane problem did not disappear.
says: Combustible renewables and waste rose from 10.2% in 1990 to 30.1% in 2024. Its energy share tripled.
Electricity access climbed from 73.2% in 1998 to 91.9% in 2024. Far more people gained power.
Waste methane emissions rose from 903.8 Mt CO2e in 1972 to 1,652 in 2024. Recovering energy did not erase emissions.
authored_explainer.closing: Calling waste renewable does not remove its emissions, so cleaner accounting still matters.
authored_explainer.question: Should waste energy count as clean?

authored_explainer.title: Population Growth Fell 54% Without Population Decline
authored_explainer.hook: Population growth fell 54%, yet the population kept increasing.
says: Rural population fell from 63.1% in 1972 to 42.2% in 2025—down to 67% of its former share.
The largest city's urban share moved from 18.2% in 1972 to 16.2% in 2025. Growth spread beyond the largest city.
Population growth fell from 2% in 1972 to 0.91% in 2025—down to 46% of its old rate.
authored_explainer.closing: Slower growth still adds people, so communities must plan for change rather than assume decline.
authored_explainer.question: How should cities plan for slower growth?
